explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but David says something much bigger. He says these men of violence "…stir up war all day long." (Psalm 140:2). Not once in a while, but all day long. I think that's why he's crying out to the LORD.
You've got it, baker. David says these men "…devise evil in their hearts and stir up war all day long." (Psalm 140:2). Not once in a while, but all day long. I think that's a heavy thing to read.
Yes, snakes. David says they "…sharpen their tongues like snakes…" (Psalm 140:3). Then he adds that the venom of vipers is on their lips. A sharp tongue with venom on it is a hard picture.

A lion's a good guess, since it's a famous fierce animal. But David picks a different animal: "They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips." (Psalm 140:3). Snakes it is, and the venom of vipers is part of the picture.

Wolves do sound dangerous, friend. But David doesn't use them here. He says, "They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips." (Psalm 140:3). Snakes it is, and the venom is part of the picture.

That's the one. These men of violence "…scheme to make me stumble." (Psalm 140:4). To scheme means it's planned, not an accident. I think David feels like somebody is out to trip him up, and he takes that straight to the LORD.

Fleeing sounds like a fair guess, friend. But David says these men "…scheme to make me stumble." (Psalm 140:4). Stumbling means getting tripped up. It's not running away. David is asking the LORD to keep him safe from the trip.

Weeping makes sense when people are against you, baker. But that's not the word David uses. He says they "…scheme to make me stumble." (Psalm 140:4). Their plan is to trip him up, and he asks the LORD to keep him safe from it.

Right on the money, baker. David says, "The proud hide a snare for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path, and lures are set out for me." (Psalm 140:5). That's a trap on the very path he walks. Somebody did some serious planning.

Stones would be a rough walk, friend, but David doesn't mention any. He says, "The proud hide a snare for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path…" (Psalm 140:5). It's a snare and a net. The snare is hidden, and the net is spread along the path.

Soldiers are a fair guess since David talks about war in this psalm. But in this verse the danger is quieter. "The proud hide a snare for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path, and lures are set out for me." (Psalm 140:5). Nobody is marching here. They're hiding things.

True, baker. With a snare hidden and a net spread along his path, David says to the LORD, "You are my God." (Psalm 140:6). Then he adds, "Hear, O LORD, my cry for help." Even with all that along his path, he talks to the LORD anyway.

Not quite, friend. David does say it, and he says it with traps set along his path. He says to the LORD, "You are my God." (Psalm 140:6). Then he asks, "Hear, O LORD, my cry for help." I'd say that's some real faith under pressure.

That's it. David says, "…You shield my head in the day of battle." (Psalm 140:7). He's talking to the LORD, whom he calls "…the strength of my salvation…" I'd take a shield over a hat any day, and I own a very tall hat.

A sword is a classic battle gear, friend. But David says nothing about one here. He says, "…You shield my head in the day of battle." (Psalm 140:7). The LORD is his protection, and the shield covers his head.

A cave sounds like a cozy plan, baker, but that's not what David says. He says, "…You shield my head in the day of battle." (Psalm 140:7). He's right there in the day of battle, and the LORD shields his head.

Oh, friend, it's the other way around. David prays, "Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; do not promote their evil plans, lest they be exalted." (Psalm 140:8). He's asking the LORD NOT to give them what they want. Handing a schemer his wish list would not be a good bake.

Right, baker. David prays, "Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; do not promote their evil plans, lest they be exalted." (Psalm 140:8). He asks the LORD to say no to their plans. Some prayers are just a very sincere "please don't."

That's exactly it. David prays, "May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused." (Psalm 140:9). The trouble is what he asks to cover their heads. It's trouble their own lips have caused.

Dust is a good guess with all this talk of battle, friend. But David prays, "May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused." (Psalm 140:9). It's trouble from their lips, not dust from a fight.

I see why you'd pick that, baker. But David's prayer is more specific: "May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused." (Psalm 140:9). The trouble comes from their own lips. The text doesn't mention the nation.

Yes! David says, "I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy." (Psalm 140:12). Notice the words "I know." After all those requests, he says what he's sure of. That's a good way to land a prayer.

Riches would be nice, friend, but that's not what David says. He says, "I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy." (Psalm 140:12). It's justice and a defender for the needy, and that matters more than a full cookie jar.

Long life is a lovely thing, baker, but it's not what David says here. He says, "I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy." (Psalm 140:12). The LORD upholds justice and defends their cause.

That's the word, baker. "Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence." (Psalm 140:13). To dwell means to live there, not just visit. David starts the psalm crying for rescue and ends it sure about that.

Trembling is a fair guess when you're in the presence of the LORD, friend. But David ends with, "Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence." (Psalm 140:13). The word is dwell, as in living in His presence.

Wandering doesn't fit this ending, baker. David says, "Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence." (Psalm 140:13). Dwell means to stay and live there. That's the opposite of wandering.
